comments.text:
On the afternoon of May 31, 2013, a cluster of storms began brewing southwest of El Reno, Oklahoma. The National Weather Service in Norman caught the sudden escalation on radar, throwing out severe warnings as the southern supercell rapidly matured. By 6:03 PM, a tornado touched down. But this wasn’t a typical funnel cloud. It was a massive, rain-wrapped multi-vortex system—a chaotic beast concealing smaller, violent suction vortices that spun like blenders within the main wedge.  
​Even worse, it defied the usual rules. Instead of tracking predictably to the northeast, it began crawling east-southeast, expanding violently by the minute.
​Amateur chaser Richard Henderson was right in its path, snapping a photo of the emerging vortex on his phone before trying to flee east down Reno Road. Nearby, chasers Brandon Sullivan and Brett Wright were caught in the rapid expansion, capturing frantic video as a stray hay bale smashed into their windshield. They barely escaped with their lives.
​Further east on Reno Road, the traffic was a mess of panicked chasers. Reed Timmer’s Dominator 2 was pushed to its limits until snapping power lines tore the hood right off the vehicle, forcing them to a halt. A mile to the south on Reuter Road, the Twistex research team—Tim Samaras, his son Paul, and Carl Young—was tracking the exact same stretch of the storm.  
​As the tornado reached Highway 81, it did something catastrophic. It swelled to an unbelievable 2.6 miles wide—becoming the largest tornado in recorded history—and abruptly hooked to the northeast, accelerating to a blinding 55 mph.  
​On Highway 81, Weather Channel meteorologist Mike Bettes and his crew were driving south, blinded by heavy rain. Before they knew it, they were engulfed by the outer edge of the monster. The winds lifted their heavy SUV and threw it 200 yards into a field. Miraculously, the crew crawled out alive.
​Others weren’t so lucky. Richard Henderson, still trying to outrun the storm on Reno Road, was caught when the tornado made its sudden northeast lurch. His car was completely destroyed, and he became the storm's first casualty.
​Meanwhile, chaser Dan Robinson was racing east down Reuter Road, trying to stay ahead of the expanding edge of the wedge. Right behind him was the Twistex crew. Robinson floored it, narrowly keeping ahead of the expanding cloud of debris. But the Twistex vehicle, trailing just a bit further back, was blindsided by a massive subvortex just west of Radio Road. The violent winds tore the car apart, tragically killing all three scientists. Robinson only survived by ditching his car further east near Evans Road and taking cover in a ditch.  
​The monster finally choked out and dissipated at 6:43 PM near Banner Road, just west of Oklahoma City. In just 40 minutes, it had reshaped the storm-chasing community forever, leaving a scar on the plains and taking eight lives—three dedicated researchers and five local citizens.

Who does not know:🌪️ El Reno 2013 was one of the most famous and powerful tornadoes ever recorded.
📅 When?
31 May 2013
Near El Reno in the Oklahoma
🌪️ What made it special?
It became the widest tornado ever measured.
At its largest, it was about 2.6 miles (4.2 km) wide.
Wind speeds were estimated to exceed 295 mph (475 km/h) in some areas.
⚠️ Why was it so dangerous?
The tornado changed direction unexpectedly.
It rapidly grew in size.
Many storm chasers were caught off guard.
😢 Tragedy
Several experienced storm chasers lost their lives, including:
Tim Samaras
Paul Samaras
Carl Young
The event changed how meteorologists and storm chasers think about tornado safety.
📡 NOVST Weather Observatory Summary
🌪️ Tornado: El Reno 2013
📏 Width: ~4.2 km (record-setting)
💨 Peak winds: ~475 km/h estimated
⚠️ Danger level: Extreme
📚 Importance: One of the most studied tornadoes in history
💀 Even veteran storm chasers said El Reno behaved unlike a typical tornado. It's often used as an example of why tornadoes should never be underestimated. 🌪️🔭
